claim: Migration of skeletal muscle precursor cells is a key step during limb muscle development.
source: Migration of skeletal muscle precursor cells is a key step during limb muscle development and depends on the activity of PAX3 and MET.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established fact in the field.

claim: Limb muscle precursor cell migration depends on the activity of PAX3 and MET.
source: Migration of skeletal muscle precursor cells is a key step during limb muscle development and depends on the activity of PAX3 and MET.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: BRAF serves a crucial function in formation of limb skeletal muscles during mouse embryogenesis downstream of MET.
source: Here, we demonstrate that BRAF serves a crucial function in formation of limb skeletal muscles during mouse embryogenesis downstream of MET and acts as a potent inducer of myoblast cell migration.
evidence: This is a primary finding demonstrated through genetic deletion experiments in mice (Pax3-Cre//Brafdel/del mutants) showing loss of limb muscle formation.

claim: BRAF acts as a potent inducer of myoblast cell migration.
source: Here, we demonstrate that BRAF serves a crucial function in formation of limb skeletal muscles during mouse embryogenesis downstream of MET and acts as a potent inducer of myoblast cell migration.
evidence: This is demonstrated through C2C12 cell migration assays showing that CA BRAF (V600E) strongly stimulates migration.

claim: A fraction of BRAF accumulates in the nucleus after activation and endosomal transport to a perinuclear position.
source: We found that a fraction of BRAF accumulates in the nucleus after activation and endosomal transport to a perinuclear position.
evidence: This is demonstrated through subcellular fractionation experiments and immunofluorescence staining showing BRAF in nuclear fractions.

claim: BRAF interacts with PAX3.
source: Mass spectrometry based screening for potential interaction partners revealed that BRAF interacts and phosphorylates PAX3.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mass spectrometry, co-immunoprecipitation, and cross-linking experiments.

claim: BRAF phosphorylates PAX3.
source: Mass spectrometry based screening for potential interaction partners revealed that BRAF interacts and phosphorylates PAX3.
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vitro kinase assays and phospho-specific antibody detection.

claim: Mutation of BRAF dependent phosphorylation sites in PAX3 impaired the ability of PAX3 to promote migration of C2C12 myoblasts.
source: Mutation of BRAF dependent phosphorylation sites in PAX3 impaired the ability of PAX3 to promote migration of C2C12 myoblasts indicating that BRAF directly activates PAX3.
evidence: This is demonstrated through migration assays using PAX3 S205A mutant which failed to stimulate migration.

claim: BRAF directly activates PAX3.
source: Mutation of BRAF dependent phosphorylation sites in PAX3 impaired the ability of PAX3 to promote migration of C2C12 myoblasts indicating that BRAF directly activates PAX3.
evidence: This is inferred from the phosphorylation data, interaction data, and functional consequences of phosphorylation site mutations.

claim: PAX3 stimulates transcription of the Met gene.
source: Since PAX3 stimulates transcription of the Met gene we propose that MET signaling via BRAF fuels a positive feedback loop, which maintains high levels of PAX3 and MET activity required for limb muscle precursor cell migration.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work (Epstein et al., 1996).

claim: MET signaling via BRAF fuels a positive feedback loop which maintains high levels of PAX3 and MET activity required for limb muscle precursor cell migration.
source: Since PAX3 stimulates transcription of the Met gene we propose that MET signaling via BRAF fuels a positive feedback loop, which maintains high levels of PAX3 and MET activity required for limb muscle precursor cell migration.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the findings that BRAF activates PAX3, PAX3 activates Met transcription, and BRAF expression increases Met and Pax3 levels.

claim: Skeletal muscles of the trunk and limbs originate from condensations of the paraxial mesoderm, the somites.
source: In vertebrates, skeletal muscles of the trunk and limbs originate from condensations of the paraxial mesoderm, the somites (Braun and Gautel, 2011; Buckingham and Relaix, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Epaxial muscles are derived from the dorso-medial part of the somatic dermomyotome.
source: Epaxial muscles are derived from the dorso-medial part of the somatic dermomyotome while the ventro-lateral part gives rise to hypaxial muscles (Ordahl and Le Douarin, 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The ventro-lateral part of the somatic dermomyotome gives rise to hypaxial muscles.
source: Epaxial muscles are derived from the dorso-medial part of the somatic dermomyotome while the ventro-lateral part gives rise to hypaxial muscles (Ordahl and Le Douarin, 1992).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Hypaxial muscles of the body wall and intercostal muscles are generated by elongation of the dermomyotomal epithelium.
source: Hypaxial muscles of the body wall and intercostal muscles are generated by elongation of the dermomyotomal epithelium.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: Muscles of the limbs, the diaphragm and the tongue are generated from a population of long-range migrating muscle precursor cells.
source: In contrast, muscles of the limbs, the diaphragm and the tongue are generated from a population of long-range migrating muscle precursor cells, which delaminate from the ventral dermomyotome at specific positions along the cranial-caudal axis after epithelial-mesenchymal transition, allowing them to form muscles far away from somites (Chevallier et al., 1977; Christ and Brand-Saberi, 2002; Christ et al., 1983).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Limb muscle precursor cells delaminate from the ventral dermomyotome at specific positions along the cranial-caudal axis after epithelial-mesenchymal transition.
source: In contrast, muscles of the limbs, the diaphragm and the tongue are generated from a population of long-range migrating muscle precursor cells, which delaminate from the ventral dermomyotome at specific positions along the cranial-caudal axis after epithelial-mesenchymal transition, allowing them to form muscles far away from somites (Chevallier et al., 1977; Christ and Brand-Saberi, 2002; Christ et al., 1983).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pax3 is required for correct formation of the ventro-lateral dermomyotome.
source: More specifically, Pax3 is required for correct formation of the ventro-lateral dermomyotome (Bober et al., 1994; Daston et al., 1996) as well as for survival (Relaix et al., 2005) and migration of limb muscle precursor cells (Daston et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Pax3 is required for survival of limb muscle precursor cells.
source: More specifically, Pax3 is required for correct formation of the ventro-lateral dermomyotome (Bober et al., 1994; Daston et al., 1996) as well as for survival (Relaix et al., 2005) and migration of limb muscle precursor cells (Daston et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Pax3 is required for migration of limb muscle precursor cells.
source: More specifically, Pax3 is required for correct formation of the ventro-lateral dermomyotome (Bober et al., 1994; Daston et al., 1996) as well as for survival (Relaix et al., 2005) and migration of limb muscle precursor cells (Daston et al., 1996).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Met is necessary for de-epithelialization and migration of limb muscle precursor cells.
source: Met is necessary for de-epithelialization and migration of limb muscle precursor cells (Bladt et al., 1995) but also for myocyte fusion (Webster and Fan, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Met is necessary for myocyte fusion.
source: Met is necessary for de-epithelialization and migration of limb muscle precursor cells (Bladt et al., 1995) but also for myocyte fusion (Webster and Fan, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: PAX3 controls expression of Met in the ventro-lateral dermomyotome.
source: It is also known that PAX3 controls expression of Met in the ventro-lateral dermomyotome (Relaix et al., 2005; Yang et al., 1996) by direct binding to the Met gene promoter (Epstein et al., 1996), thereby enabling delamination and migration of limb muscle precursor cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: PAX3 controls Met expression by direct binding to the Met gene promoter.
source: It is also known that PAX3 controls expression of Met in the ventro-lateral dermomyotome (Relaix et al., 2005; Yang et al., 1996) by direct binding to the Met gene promoter (Epstein et al., 1996), thereby enabling delamination and migration of limb muscle precursor cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Germ line inactivation of Braf results in embryonic lethality between E10.5 and E12.5.
source: To answer these questions we inactivated the Braf gene specifically in limb muscle precursor cells, since germ line inactivation of Braf results in embryonic lethality between E10.5 and E12.5 and causes multiple defects including growth retardation, vascular and neuronal defects (Wojnowski et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Germ line inactivation of Braf causes multiple defects including growth retardation, vascular and neuronal defects.
source: To answer these questions we inactivated the Braf gene specifically in limb muscle precursor cells, since germ line inactivation of Braf results in embryonic lethality between E10.5 and E12.5 and causes multiple defects including growth retardation, vascular and neuronal defects (Wojnowski et al., 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: HGF robustly induced migration of C2C12 cells.
source: We found that HGF, the ligand of the MET receptor, robustly induced migration of C2C12 cells.
evidence: This is demonstrated through migration assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Stimulation of C2C12 migration by HGF was blocked by knockdown of Met.
source: Stimulation of migration was blocked by knockdown of Met demonstrating that C2C12 cells can be utilized to study the mechanisms of MET receptor signaling for migration of myogenic cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: C2C12 cells can be utilized to study the mechanisms of MET receptor signaling for migration of myogenic cells.
source: Stimulation of migration was blocked by knockdown of Met demonstrating that C2C12 cells can be utilized to study the mechanisms of MET receptor signaling for migration of myogenic cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that HGF-induced migration is Met-dependent in C2C12 cells.

claim: Knockdown of Braf essentially phenocopied the effects of Met receptor knockdown on C2C12 cell migration.
source: Systematic analysis of the role of potential downstream effectors of MET signaling by siRNA-mediated knockdown disclosed an important role of the serine/threonine-specific protein kinase BRAF, which essentially phenocopied the effects of Met receptor knockdown (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Knockdown of Pax3 inhibited HGF-mediated stimulation of C2C12 cell migration.
source: Interestingly, knockdown of Pax3 did also inhibit HGF-mediated stimulation of C2C12 cell migration suggesting a functional involvement of PAX3 in MET signaling (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CA BRAF (V600E) strongly stimulated migration of C2C12 cells.
source: We observed a strong stimulation of migration by CA BRAF (V600E) and -to a lesser extent- WT BRAF while expression of CRAF had only minor effects on muscle cell migration (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through transfection and migration assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: WT BRAF stimulated migration of C2C12 cells to a lesser extent than CA BRAF (V600E).
source: We observed a strong stimulation of migration by CA BRAF (V600E) and -to a lesser extent- WT BRAF while expression of CRAF had only minor effects on muscle cell migration (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through transfection and migration assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Expression of CRAF had only minor effects on muscle cell migration.
source: We observed a strong stimulation of migration by CA BRAF (V600E) and -to a lesser extent- WT BRAF while expression of CRAF had only minor effects on muscle cell migration (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through transfection and migration assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: CA BRAF (V600E) and WT BRAF stimulated expression of Pax3 and Met in C2C12 cells.
source: CA BRAF (V600E) and WT BRAF also stimulated expression of Pax3 and Met in C2C12 cells adding further evidence to the putative role of BRAF in the regulatory loop controlling migration of myogenic cells (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: RCAS virus-mediated expression of BRAF increased cellular migration out of somitic explants isolated from chicken embryos.
source: We found that RCAS virus-mediated expression of BRAF and PAX3 but not human alkaline phosphatase (AP) increased cellular migration out of somitic explants isolated from chicken embryos and cultivated in matrigel further corroborating the results obtained with C2C12 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through explant culture experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: RCAS virus-mediated expression of PAX3 increased cellular migration out of somitic explants isolated from chicken embryos.
source: We found that RCAS virus-mediated expression of BRAF and PAX3 but not human alkaline phosphatase (AP) increased cellular migration out of somitic explants isolated from chicken embryos and cultivated in matrigel further corroborating the results obtained with C2C12 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through explant culture experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Human alkaline phosphatase (AP) did not increase cellular migration out of somitic explants.
source: We found that RCAS virus-mediated expression of BRAF and PAX3 but not human alkaline phosphatase (AP) increased cellular migration out of somitic explants isolated from chicken embryos and cultivated in matrigel further corroborating the results obtained with C2C12 cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through explant culture experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of the MEK1/2 inhibitor UO126 had only minor effects on BRAF-induced migration.
source: Surprisingly, addition of the MEK1/2 inhibitor UO126 had only minor effects on migration, although the increase in ERK1/2 phosphorylation after transfection of WT and CA BRAF (V600E) was efficiently prevented by the inhibitor (Figure 1C,D) indicating a MEK/ERK independent mechanism of BRAF signaling.
evidence: This is demonstrated through migration assays with UO126 treatment shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: UO126 efficiently prevented the increase in ERK1/2 phosphorylation after transfection of WT and CA BRAF (V600E).
source: Surprisingly, addition of the MEK1/2 inhibitor UO126 had only minor effects on migration, although the increase in ERK1/2 phosphorylation after transfection of WT and CA BRAF (V600E) was efficiently prevented by the inhibitor (Figure 1C,D) indicating a MEK/ERK independent mechanism of BRAF signaling.
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: BRAF signaling for migration operates through a MEK/ERK independent mechanism.
source: Surprisingly, addition of the MEK1/2 inhibitor UO126 had only minor effects on migration, although the increase in ERK1/2 phosphorylation after transfection of WT and CA BRAF (V600E) was efficiently prevented by the inhibitor (Figure 1C,D) indicating a MEK/ERK independent mechanism of BRAF signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that MEK inhibition blocks ERK phosphorylation but not migration.

claim: Addition of Dynasore significantly prevented BRAF dependent stimulation of migration when the constitutively active form of BRAF was used.
source: Interestingly, addition of Dynasore, a pharmacological inhibitor of endosomal trafficking, significantly prevented BRAF dependent stimulation of migration when the constitutively active form of BRAF was used in the experiments (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through migration assays with Dynasore treatment shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining confirmed the absence of BRAF protein in the dermomyotome of Pax3-Cre//Brafdel/del mutant embryos at E10.5.
source: Immunofluorescence staining using an anti-BRAF antibody confirmed the absence of BRAF protein in the dermomyotome of Pax3-Cre//Brafdel/del mutant embryos at E10.5 while the dermomyotome of WT control embryos was strongly positive for BRAF (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Germ line inactivation of Braf (Brafdel/del) resulted in arrest of limb muscle precursor cell migration.
source: Importantly, germ line inactivation (Brafdel/del) as well as deletion of Braf in Pax3-expressing limb muscle precursor cells (Pax3-Cre//Brafdel/del) resulted in arrest of cell migration as indicated by the absence of PAX3+-cells in the developing forelimb buds at E10.5 (Figure 3A,B), which was further validated by immunofluorescence analysis of PAX3+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and RT-PCR analysis of Met and Pax3 expression (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through whole mount in situ hybridization and immunofluorescence shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of Braf in Pax3-expressing limb muscle precursor cells (Pax3-Cre//Brafdel/del) resulted in arrest of cell migration.
source: Importantly, germ line inactivation (Brafdel/del) as well as deletion of Braf in Pax3-expressing limb muscle precursor cells (Pax3-Cre//Brafdel/del) resulted in arrest of cell migration as indicated by the absence of PAX3+-cells in the developing forelimb buds at E10.5 (Figure 3A,B), which was further validated by immunofluorescence analysis of PAX3+ cells (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and RT-PCR analysis of Met and Pax3 expression (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through whole mount in situ hybridization, immunofluorescence, and RT-PCR shown in Figures 2C, 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only very few Braf-deficient PAX3+-cells delaminated from the dermomyotome and initiated migration.
source: Closer inspection of the PAX3 immunofluorescence staining revealed that only very few Braf-deficient PAX3+-cells delaminated from the dermomyotome and initiated migration suggesting a requirement of Braf for epithelia-mesenchymal transition of dermomyotomal cells and/or migration (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: There was a virtually complete absence of Myod and Myf5 expressing myogenic cells in limb buds of E10.5 Pax3-Cre//Brafdel/del embryos.
source: We also found a virtually complete absence of Myod and Myf5 expressing myogenic cells in limb buds of E10.5 Pax3-Cre//Brafdel/del embryos (Figure 3C), although we noted a reduced expression at later stages by Western blot analysis (Figure 2D) indicating that a small population of Braf-deficient limb muscle progenitor cells was able to reach its target.
evidence: This is demonstrated through whole mount in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3C.

claim: A small population of Braf-deficient limb muscle progenitor cells was able to reach its target at later stages.
source: We also found a virtually complete absence of Myod and Myf5 expressing myogenic cells in limb buds of E10.5 Pax3-Cre//Brafdel/del embryos (Figure 3C), although we noted a reduced expression at later stages by Western blot analysis (Figure 2D) indicating that a small population of Braf-deficient limb muscle progenitor cells was able to reach its target.
evidence: This is inferred from the detection of reduced but present myogenic markers at E14.5 shown in Figure 2D.

claim: There was a major reduction of forelimb muscles at E14.5 in Pax3-Cre//Brafdel/del embryos.
source: Accordingly, we observed a major reduction of forelimb muscles at later stages of development (E14.5), which was more pronounced in the distal compared to the proximal parts of the limb, where some residual muscle formation was seen (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence and histological analysis shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: The reduction of forelimb muscles in Pax3-Cre//Brafdel/del embryos was more pronounced in the distal compared to the proximal parts of the limb.
source: Accordingly, we observed a major reduction of forelimb muscles at later stages of development (E14.5), which was more pronounced in the distal compared to the proximal parts of the limb, where some residual muscle formation was seen (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence and histological analysis shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: There was no significant increase in the number of apoptotic cells in Braf mutant compared to WT control embryos at E10.5.
source: In contrast, we did not observe a significant increase in the number of apoptotic cells in Braf mutant compared to WT control embryos at E10.5 suggesting that the loss of Braf in dermomyotomal cells does not lead to programmed cell death (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through TUNEL staining shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Loss of Braf in dermomyotomal cells does not lead to programmed cell death.
source: In contrast, we did not observe a significant increase in the number of apoptotic cells in Braf mutant compared to WT control embryos at E10.5 suggesting that the loss of Braf in dermomyotomal cells does not lead to programmed cell death (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is inferred from the absence of increased TUNEL staining in mutant embryos.

claim: There was no reduction of CD31-positive endothelial cells in Braf mutant limb buds.
source: However, similar to the presence of normal numbers of endothelial progenitor cells in Pax3 mutant embryos (Yvernogeau et al., 2012), we did not observe a reduction of CD31-positive endothelial cells in Braf mutant limb buds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) indicating that KDR does not critically rely on BRAF for promoting endothelial precursor cell migration.
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: KDR does not critically rely on BRAF for promoting endothelial precursor cell migration.
source: However, similar to the presence of normal numbers of endothelial progenitor cells in Pax3 mutant embryos (Yvernogeau et al., 2012), we did not observe a reduction of CD31-positive endothelial cells in Braf mutant limb buds (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) indicating that KDR does not critically rely on BRAF for promoting endothelial precursor cell migration.
evidence: This is inferred from the normal presence of endothelial cells in Braf mutant limb buds.

claim: Co-transfection of the Pax3 reporter plasmid together with Pax3 and Braf or CA Braf (V600E) into HEK293T cells revealed a strong increase of transcriptional activity.
source: Co-transfection of the Pax3 reporter plasmid together with Pax3 and Braf or CA Braf (V600E) into HEK293T cells revealed a strong increase of transcriptional activity, resulting in an up to 15-fold change when CA Braf (V600E) was used (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 2F.

claim: CA Braf (V600E) resulted in an up to 15-fold increase in PAX3 transcriptional activity.
source: Co-transfection of the Pax3 reporter plasmid together with Pax3 and Braf or CA Braf (V600E) into HEK293T cells revealed a strong increase of transcriptional activity, resulting in an up to 15-fold change when CA Braf (V600E) was used (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is demonstrated through luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis of immunoprecipitated samples from WT limb buds of E10.5 mouse embryos using an antibody against endogenous BRAF identified PAX3 and PAX7 as potential interaction partners of BRAF.
source: Importantly, mass spectrometry analysis of immunoprecipitated samples from WT limb buds of E10.5 mouse embryos using an antibody against endogenous BRAF identified -among several other proteins- the nuclear transcription factors PAX3 and PAX7 as potential interaction partners of BRAF (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Coupled immunoprecipitation-Western blot analysis confirmed the physical interaction between BRAF and 53 kDa PAX3.
source: Coupled immunoprecipitation-Western blot analysis of samples from E10.5 limb buds using either BRAF antibodies for IP and PAX3 antibodies for Western blot or vice versa further confirmed the physical interaction between BRAF and 53 kDa PAX3 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Comparative GST pull-down assays revealed a significantly stronger interaction of the constitutively active compared to the WT form of BRAF with GST-PAX3.
source: Comparative GST pull-down assays of extracts from C2C12 cells transfected either with WT Braf or CA Braf (V600E) revealed a significantly stronger interaction of the constitutively active compared to the WT form of BRAF with GST-PAX3 (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through GST pull-down assays shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Cross-linking experiments detected an additional single band at ca. 150 kDa corresponding to the cross-linked BRAF-PAX3 heteromer.
source: Moreover, either antibody detected an additional single band at ca. 150 kDa, which corresponds to the cross-linked BRAF-PAX3 heteromer.
evidence: This is demonstrated through cross-linking experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Cleavage of the spacer with DTT severed the cross-linked BRAF-PAX3 complex.
source: Cleavage of the spacer with DTT severed the cross-linked BRAF-PAX3 complex, further verifying identity of the band (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through cross-linking experiments with DTT treatment shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Subcellular fractionation of C2C12 cells disclosed the presence of a minor amount of endogenous BRAF in the nucleus.
source: Subcellular fractionation of C2C12 cells disclosed the presence of a minor amount of endogenous BRAF in the nucleus although the major share of BRAF was present in the cytoplasm (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through subcellular fractionation and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The major share of BRAF was present in the cytoplasm.
source: Subcellular fractionation of C2C12 cells disclosed the presence of a minor amount of endogenous BRAF in the nucleus although the major share of BRAF was present in the cytoplasm (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through subcellular fractionation and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PAX3 was exclusively found in the nuclear fraction.
source: In contrast, PAX3 was exclusively found in the nuclear fraction, even after expression of large amounts of HA-tagged Pax3.
evidence: This is demonstrated through subcellular fractionation and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The concentration of BRAF in the nuclear fraction increased when CA Braf (V600E) was transfected into cells.
source: The concentration of BRAF in the nuclear fraction increased when CA Braf (V600E) was transfected into cells irrespective of the presence or absence of HGF.
evidence: This is demonstrated through subcellular fractionation and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The nuclear level of BRAF decreased when endosomal trafficking was blocked by administration of Dynasore.
source: Interestingly, the nuclear level of BRAF decreased when endosomal trafficking was blocked by administration of Dynasore (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through subcellular fractionation with Dynasore treatment shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Co-immunoprecipitation experiments using only the nuclear fraction of transfected C2C12 cells corroborated the interaction of nuclear BRAF with PAX3 in the absence of cytosolic BRAF.
source: We also conducted additional co-immunoprecipitation experiments using only the nuclear fraction of transfected C2C12 cells, which corroborated the interaction of nuclear BRAF with PAX3 in the absence of cytosolic BRAF (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through co-immunoprecipitation of nuclear fractions shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Immunofluorescence staining revealed a striking co-localization of PAX3 and BRAF in nuclei of limb muscle precursor cells.
source: Finally, we performed immunofluorescence staining for PAX3 and BRAF using mouse embryonic tissues or C2C12 cells transfected with Braf, CA Braf (V600E) and Pax3. We observed a striking co-localization of PAX3 and BRAF in nuclei of limb muscle precursor cells and strong signals for P-BRAF in nuclei of transfected cells although localization of P-BRAF in the cytoplasm dominated (Figure 5C,D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence analysis shown in Figure 5C,D.

claim: Co-staining for P-BRAF and the endosomal marker EEA1 revealed a close association of endosomal vesicle and P-BRAF in the cytoplasm but not in the nucleus.
source: Co-staining for P-BRAF and the endosomal marker EEA1 revealed a close association of endosomal vesicle and P-BRAF in the cytoplasm but not in the nucleus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated through immunofluorescence co-staining shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockdown of Eea1 resulted in decreased levels of nuclear BRAF.
source: Knockdown of Eea1 resulted in decreased levels of nuclear BRAF while siErk1/2 showed little effects (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through siRNA knockdown and subcellular fractionation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: siErk1/2 showed little effects on nuclear BRAF levels.
source: Knockdown of Eea1 resulted in decreased levels of nuclear BRAF while siErk1/2 showed little effects (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through siRNA knockdown and subcellular fractionation shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Knockdown of Eea1, dynamin-2 (Dnm2), clathrin heavy chain (Cltc), caveolin-1 (Cav1) and ADP ribosylation factor 6 (Arf6) did not significantly affect the phosphorylation level of ERK1/2.
source: To explore whether disruption of endosomal trafficking does not only inhibit transport of BRAF into the nucleus but also activation of ERK1/2 we knocked down Eea1, dynamin-2 (Dnm2), clathrin heavy chain (Cltc), caveolin-1 (Cav1) and ADP ribosylation factor 6 (Arf6). In neither case we observed significant effects on the phosphorylation level of ERK1/2 while knock down of Braf or Erk1/2 resulted in a strong reduction of ERK1/2 phosphorylation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through siRNA knockdown and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Knock down of Braf or Erk1/2 resulted in a strong reduction of ERK1/2 phosphorylation.
source: To explore whether disruption of endosomal trafficking does not only inhibit transport of BRAF into the nucleus but also activation of ERK1/2 we knocked down Eea1, dynamin-2 (Dnm2), clathrin heavy chain (Cltc), caveolin-1 (Cav1) and ADP ribosylation factor 6 (Arf6). In neither case we observed significant effects on the phosphorylation level of ERK1/2 while knock down of Braf or Erk1/2 resulted in a strong reduction of ERK1/2 phosphorylation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through siRNA knockdown and Western blot analysis shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Knockdown of Eea1 but not of Erk1/2 significantly inhibited BRAF-mediated stimulation of C2C12 cell migration.
source: Furthermore, knockdown of Eea1 but not of Erk1/2 significantly inhibited BRAF-mediated stimulation of C2C12 cell migration (Figure 6C) supporting our conclusion that signaling events downstream of MET necessary for limb muscle precursor migration rely on the translocation of BRAF into the nucleus and not on the activation of the ERK1/2 signaling cascade.
evidence: This is demonstrated through siRNA knockdown and migration assays shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Signaling events downstream of MET necessary for limb muscle precursor migration rely on the translocation of BRAF into the nucleus and not on the activation of the ERK1/2 signaling cascade.
source: Furthermore, knockdown of Eea1 but not of Erk1/2 significantly inhibited BRAF-mediated stimulation of C2C12 cell migration (Figure 6C) supporting our conclusion that signaling events downstream of MET necessary for limb muscle precursor migration rely on the translocation of BRAF into the nucleus and not on the activation of the ERK1/2 signaling cascade.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of Eea1 vs Erk1/2 knockdown on migration.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis identified multiple new phosphorylation sites at serine and threonine residues in PAX3.
source: Subsequent fractionation of FASP-digested PAX3 peptides by cation-exchange liquid chromatography followed by mass spectrometry analysis using a quadrupole-based Q Exactive instrument identified multiple new phosphorylation sites at serine and threonine residues as well as five phosphorylation sites (at Ser180, Ser187, Ser201, Ser205 and Ser209), which had already been reported before (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Mass spectrometry analysis identified five phosphorylation sites in PAX3 (at Ser180, Ser187, Ser201, Ser205 and Ser209) which had already been reported before.
source: Subsequent fractionation of FASP-digested PAX3 peptides by cation-exchange liquid chromatography followed by mass spectrometry analysis using a quadrupole-based Q Exactive instrument identified multiple new phosphorylation sites at serine and threonine residues as well as five phosphorylation sites (at Ser180, Ser187, Ser201, Ser205 and Ser209), which had already been reported before (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through mass spectrometry analysis shown in Figure 7A and comparison with published data.

claim: Transfection of Braf primarily increased PAX3 phosphorylation at Ser222.
source: We found that transfection of Braf primarily increased PAX3 phosphorylation at Ser222 while phosphorylation at the other sites was not prominently enhanced when normalized to PAX3 protein concentrations (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through quantitative SILAC mass spectrometry shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: The S205A Pax3 mutant failed to stimulate muscle cell migration when co-transfected with CA Braf (V600E).
source: The S205A Pax3 mutant failed to stimulate muscle cell migration while S201A, S209A and S222A mutants had no discernable effects compared to WT Pax3 indicating that phosphorylation of Ser205 is instrumental for PAX3-dependent stimulation of muscle cell migration (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through migration assays with PAX3 mutants shown in Figure 8A.

claim: S201A, S209A and S222A PAX3 mutants had no discernable effects on migration compared to WT Pax3.
source: The S205A Pax3 mutant failed to stimulate muscle cell migration while S201A, S209A and S222A mutants had no discernable effects compared to WT Pax3 indicating that phosphorylation of Ser205 is instrumental for PAX3-dependent stimulation of muscle cell migration (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through migration assays with PAX3 mutants shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Phosphorylation of Ser205 is instrumental for PAX3-dependent stimulation of muscle cell migration.
source: The S205A Pax3 mutant failed to stimulate muscle cell migration while S201A, S209A and S222A mutants had no discernable effects compared to WT Pax3 indicating that phosphorylation of Ser205 is instrumental for PAX3-dependent stimulation of muscle cell migration (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is inferred from the specific loss of function of the S205A mutant.

claim: BRAF induced phosphorylation of PAX3 at Ser205 in both HEK293T and C2C12 muscle cells.
source: Therefore, we transfected Pax3 together with CA Braf (V600E) into HEK293T and C2C12 muscle cells, but this time monitored phosphorylation of PAX3 using an antibody specific for p-Ser205. We found that BRAF clearly induced phosphorylation of PAX3 at Ser205 in both cell types (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through Western blot analysis with phospho-specific antibody shown in Figure 8B.

claim: In vitro kinase assay corroborated that BRAF directly phosphorylates PAX3 at Ser205.
source: Furthermore, we performed an in vitro kinase assay using recombinant BRAF and bacterially produced, affinity-purified GST-PAX3. Western blot analysis using the p-Ser205 specific PAX3-antibody corroborated that BRAF directly phosphorylates PAX3 at Ser205 (Figure 8C, upper panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vitro kinase assays shown in Figure 8C.

claim: All mutant PAX3 proteins, with the exception of S205A, reacted with the p-Ser205 PAX3 antibody after incubation with BRAF.
source: To analyze the specificity of the p-Ser205 PAX3-antibody we performed in vitro kinase assays using the S201A, S205A, S209A and S222A PAX3-mutants as substrates. As expected all mutant PAX3 proteins, with the exception of S205A, reacted with the p-Ser205 PAX3 antibody after incubation with BRAF demonstrating specificity of the antibody (Figure 8C, lower panel).
evidence: This is demonstrated through in vitro kinase assays with PAX3 mutants shown in Figure 8C.

claim: BRAF phosphorylates PAX3 at multiple sites.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that BRAF phosphorylates PAX3 at multiple sites but that phosphorylation at Ser205 is critical for efficient PAX3-dependent stimulation of muscle cell migration.
evidence: This is demonstrated through mass spectrometry and in vitro kinase assays.

claim: Phosphorylation at Ser205 is critical for efficient PAX3-dependent stimulation of muscle cell migration.
source: Taken together, our results suggest that BRAF phosphorylates PAX3 at multiple sites but that phosphorylation at Ser205 is critical for efficient PAX3-dependent stimulation of muscle cell migration.
evidence: This is demonstrated through functional assays with the S205A mutant.

claim: BRAF is critical for migration of limb muscle precursor cells.
source: Here, we demonstrate that BRAF is critical for migration of limb muscle precursor cells, which serves an essential role for normal limb muscle development.
evidence: This is demonstrated through genetic deletion experiments and migration assays.

claim: Migration of limb muscle precursor cells serves an essential role for normal limb muscle development.
source: Here, we demonstrate that BRAF is critical for migration of limb muscle precursor cells, which serves an essential role for normal limb muscle development.
evidence: This is established knowledge and demonstrated by the severe limb muscle defects in Braf mutants.

claim: BRAF acts downstream of GAB1 to mediate intracellular MET signaling.
source: Targeted mutation of Braf in migrating limb muscle precursor cells partially phenocopied effects of inactivation of the receptor tyrosine kinase Met and its large adaptor protein GAB1 indicating that BRAF acts downstream of GAB1 to mediate intracellular MET signaling.
evidence: This is inferred from the phenotypic similarity between Braf, Met, and Gab1 mutants.

claim: A fraction of BRAF enters the nucleus where it binds and activates the transcription factor PAX3.
source: Furthermore, we show that a fraction of BRAF enters the nucleus, where it binds and activates the transcription factor PAX3 thereby creating a shortcut bypassing established signaling pathways.
evidence: This is demonstrated through subcellular fractionation, immunofluorescence, and functional assays.

claim: BRAF creates a shortcut bypassing established signaling pathways.
source: Furthermore, we show that a fraction of BRAF enters the nucleus, where it binds and activates the transcription factor PAX3 thereby creating a shortcut bypassing established signaling pathways.
evidence: This is inferred from the MEK/ERK-independent mechanism of BRAF action on migration.

claim: MET undergoes rapid endocytosis in a process called 'endosomal signaling' and traffics through peripheral endosomes to a perinuclear localization.
source: Since MET undergoes rapid endocytosis in a process called 'endosomal signaling' and traffics through peripheral endosomes to a perinuclear localization (Barrow-McGee and Kermorgant, 2014), we investigated whether inhibition of endosomal trafficking abrogates the effects of BRAF on migration of C2C12 muscle cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: MET-induced activation of STAT3 within the perinuclear compartment allows efficient activation and nuclear accumulation of STAT3.
source: MET-induced activation of STAT3 within the perinuclear compartment allows efficient activation and nuclear accumulation of STAT3 (Kermorgant and Parker, 2008) suggesting that trafficking and 'endosomal signaling' of MET enables direct transfer of signaling complexes to their intended target (Miaczynska et al., 2004b) thereby favoring distinct signaling events.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Trafficking and 'endosomal signaling' of MET enables direct transfer of signaling complexes to their intended target.
source: MET-induced activation of STAT3 within the perinuclear compartment allows efficient activation and nuclear accumulation of STAT3 (Kermorgant and Parker, 2008) suggesting that trafficking and 'endosomal signaling' of MET enables direct transfer of signaling complexes to their intended target (Miaczynska et al., 2004b) thereby favoring distinct signaling events.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Internalization and perinuclear accumulation of MET is instrumental for transport of a fraction of BRAF into the nucleus.
source: Our finding that MET co-localizes with BRAF in EEA1+ endosomes after HGF stimulation and that blockage of endosomal trafficking prevents accumulation of BRAF in the nucleus indicates that internalization and perinuclear accumulation of MET is instrumental for transport of a fraction of BRAF into the nucleus.
evidence: This is inferred from the co-localization data and the effects of endosomal trafficking inhibition.

claim: The PAX3 protein is posttranslationally modified by acetylation.
source: The PAX3 protein is posttranslationally modified by acetylation (Ichi et al., 2011), ubiquitination (Boutet et al., 2007), and phosphorylation (Amstutz et al., 2008; Iyengar et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The PAX3 protein is posttranslationally modified by ubiquitination.
source: The PAX3 protein is posttranslationally modified by acetylation (Ichi et al., 2011), ubiquitination (Boutet et al., 2007), and phosphorylation (Amstutz et al., 2008; Iyengar et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The PAX3 protein is posttranslationally modified by phosphorylation.
source: The PAX3 protein is posttranslationally modified by acetylation (Ichi et al., 2011), ubiquitination (Boutet et al., 2007), and phosphorylation (Amstutz et al., 2008; Iyengar et al., 2012; Miller et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: CK2 can phosphorylate PAX3 at Ser205 and Ser209.
source: So far, two different kinases were identified to phosphorylate PAX3: GSK3β and CK2. CK2 seems able to phosphorylate Ser205 and Ser209 (Iyengar et al., 2012) while GSK3β was found to phosphorylate Ser201, Ser205 and possibly Ser197 (Kubic et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: GSK3β phosphorylates PAX3 at Ser201, Ser205 and possibly Ser197.
source: So far, two different kinases were identified to phosphorylate PAX3: GSK3β and CK2. CK2 seems able to phosphorylate Ser205 and Ser209 (Iyengar et al., 2012) while GSK3β was found to phosphorylate Ser201, Ser205 and possibly Ser197 (Kubic et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The octapeptide domain of PAX3 mediates interaction with GROUCHO.
source: In fact, the octapeptide domain close to Ser205 mediates interaction of PAX3 with GROUCHO, which prevents transcriptional activation of PAX3 targets during melanocyte and neural cell differentiation (Lang et al., 2005; Muhr et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: GROUCHO prevents transcriptional activation of PAX3 targets during melanocyte and neural cell differentiation.
source: In fact, the octapeptide domain close to Ser205 mediates interaction of PAX3 with GROUCHO, which prevents transcriptional activation of PAX3 targets during melanocyte and neural cell differentiation (Lang et al., 2005; Muhr et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Activation of PAX3 by overexpression of WT and CA Braf (V600E) in C2C12 muscle cells results in marked up-regulation of Met and Pax3.
source: Importantly, we found that activation of PAX3 by overexpression of WT and CA Braf (V600E) in C2C12 muscle cells results in marked up-regulation of Met and Pax3.
evidence: This is demonstrated through RT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claim: WT and CA Braf (V600E) increased the transcriptional activity of PAX3 in Luciferase reporter assays on HEK293T cells.
source: Similarly, WT and CA Braf (V600E) increased the transcriptional activity of PAX3 in Luciferase reporter assays on HEK293T cells, which fits to the proposed role of PAX3 to stimulate Met expression in myogenic cells (Epstein et al., 1996) and to activate its own expression by direct positive autoregulation (Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is demonstrated through luciferase reporter assays shown in Figure 2F.

claim: PAX3 activates its own expression by direct positive autoregulation.
source: Similarly, WT and CA Braf (V600E) increased the transcriptional activity of PAX3 in Luciferase reporter assays on HEK293T cells, which fits to the proposed role of PAX3 to stimulate Met expression in myogenic cells (Epstein et al., 1996) and to activate its own expression by direct positive autoregulation (Moore et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.
